Hypercasual Teardown

Number Master: Run and merge

You are the number. Everything on the road is a number too — blue if you can swallow it, red if it can swallow you — and every swallow, every gate and every upgrade moves that line.

A one-thumb portrait runner by KAYAC. Drag a chunky blue number down a white sky-track, eat what is not bigger than you, pay a subtraction gate, dodge saws and gaps, then ram a staircase of numbered walls. How high you climb is paid out as cash, which buys a bigger starting number or a better payout multiplier for the next level.

  • KAYAC Inc. · Android & iOS
  • Launched Oct 2022
  • 100M+ Google Play downloads
  • Free · ads
  • One level ≈ 20 s of steering

1Colour is a comparison, recomputed every frame

The game has one rule and paints it on every object: a road number is blue while it is not bigger than you and red once it is. Because your number changes constantly, the whole road re-colours under you.

Road number ≤ your number → blue · swallow it, add it   Road number > your number → red · touch it and you break Equality counts as safe: with a starting value of 5, the road's 5s are already blue.
Before · starting value 5
After · mid-run at 86

Why the rule carries the whole game

Compare this frame with the hero image: same three lanes, a second apart. At 65 the 77s were lethal; at 115 they are a meal. Nothing on the road has a fixed meaning. Safety is a relation between two numbers, and the player is one of them.

That relation produces every interesting situation in the game. Swallowing in the right order makes later objects safe (a ladder of 1, 2, 4, 8 … 128 is eaten bottom-up). Paying a gate can make a safe object lethal again (section 3). A starting-number upgrade turns the first rows of a level blue before the run begins (section 6). The colour is the only tutorial the game needs, and it is always correct for the current instant.

Swallowing is immediate: touching a blue number removes it and adds its face value; four 50s take 65 to 115, 165, 215 and 265 in about a second and a half. Touching a red one ends the attempt on contact.

2One level, end to end

A level is a single straight sprint with no pause between decisions: about twenty seconds of steering, a few seconds of smashing, a payout, and the next level is already waiting.

  1. Pre-runNumber waits on the road; two upgrade cards; a hand sweeps left-right.until first drag
  2. RunAuto-forward; drag sideways to eat blue, avoid red, pick gates, hit pads.≈15–25 s
  3. Finish lineCheckered strip; the road becomes a staircase of numbered walls.instant
  4. Smash & stopEvery wall ≤ your number bursts; the first bigger wall stops you: “Level Complete”.≈2–4 s
  5. PayoutThe number drains into cash: number × INCOME.≈1.5 s drain
  6. Next levelLevel counter +1, new road, cards updated.≈4.5 s after the stop
  7. FailureRed contact or a fall: number breaks, “Failed...”, same level back at its pre-run. No cost.≈2.5 s to retry

The first minute teaches by paving

A fresh install opens with a terms prompt over the very first road: Level 1, a blue 2, a gesturing hand and five columns of 1s and 2s. Every early object is safe, so the first drag cannot fail; the player learns that touching numbers makes the number bigger before ever seeing red. Red appears further along Level 1 as a side column and a single larger blocker, so the first lethal read comes with a comfortable margin.

The upgrade cards sit on the road itself rather than in a menu. After the first payout they are the only thing between levels, which makes “buy, then drag” the default rhythm. Starting a run needs nothing more than putting a thumb on the road and moving it.

Durations come from two edited gameplay recordings at normal speed; they are approximate, not input-latency measurements.

3Gates spend the number you built — and move the line

Subtraction gates come in pairs or banks split by a purple divider. Every lane is an exit with a price, and the real price is not the label: it is what the lower number can no longer touch on the other side.

A gate is paid over time, not in one tick

Entering a gate does not subtract instantly. The number and the gate's label count down together while blue chips fly off the number, and the gate is spent when its label reaches zero. A −555 gate takes roughly a second and a half to cross. The player sees the cost being paid, and sees the moment the number drops under something ahead.

That makes gate choice the game's sharpest decision. The cheaper gate is usually right, but layouts deliberately place a number just above the expensive lane's result, or hide a red number directly behind the cheap-looking gate. The colour of that hidden number flips while the player is still inside the gate — too late to steer away.

Whether a gate can take the number to zero or below is never shown; every crossing seen leaves at least 10.

4Failure is one number short — or one step off the edge

There are two ways to lose and both are instant: touch a red number, or leave the track. Neither costs anything but the attempt; the same level is back on screen in about two and a half seconds.

Why losing stays cheap and still stings

A failed attempt keeps cash, upgrades and level number. What it takes is the run's growth: a number that had reached a thousand is back at its starting value. The sting is the near miss — 144 against a red 150 in one recording, 1111 slipping off the track one step before the finish in another — not a penalty.

Restarting on the pre-run screen is quietly important: after a failure the player sees the upgrade cards again, and a single START NUMBER purchase may be exactly what turns the blocker that killed them blue next time. The failure → shop → retry loop is the economy's most persuasive moment.

Edges are the second danger type. Narrow bridges, raised lanes and gaps appear from the earliest levels; nothing marks an edge except the end of the white surface, and a fall reads just as fast as a collision.

5The staircase turns size into money

After the finish line nothing can kill you. The road climbs a staircase of numbered walls under a giant x777 crown; the number rams through every wall it equals or beats, stops at the first bigger one, and that is the level's result.

Payout = final number × INCOME, rounded up   1053 × x1.3 = +1369 Checked against the wallet: 1,583 → 2,952 for 1053 at x1.3; 1,411 → 9,481 for 4035 at x2.0. The wall you stop at decides how the climb looks, not the cash.

The staircase does two jobs. It is a gauge — the walls are a ruler printed in the world, so the player sees how big their number was in terms of how much it destroyed. And it is the money moment: the number literally pours into the wallet. Because pay depends on the exact final number rather than the last wall broken, every swallowed 1 still counts, and gates are measured in lost cash as well as lost safety.

The crown is the game's horizon. Walls seen in the recordings include 100, 200, 300, 400 … 800, then 1200, 1400, 1800 and 4500; the crown above is never touched in either recording, and player reviews describe it as unattainable even with maxed upgrades.

6Two cards run the whole economy

Between levels the player has exactly two purchases. One makes the road friendlier, the other makes the result pay more — and both stop at a printed maximum.

Affordable · white price
Unaffordable · pink price

START NUMBER buys access; INCOME buys money

START NUMBER adds 1 to the value the number begins each level with. A single point sounds trivial next to final numbers in the thousands, but levels place their first rows and blockers just above the default start, so each point can turn a lethal opening into a meal and let the snowball begin earlier. Buying it re-colours the road immediately on the pre-run screen.

INCOME adds 0.1 to the payout multiplier, so it converts directly into cash on every future level.

START NUMBER→bluer opening→bigger final number→× INCOME→cash→next card

Prices climb steadily (table below) while income per level grows only with the multiplier and the player's routes, so in natural play purchases come in small batches every few levels. Both cards end: START NUMBER at MAX:100, INCOME at MAX:x6.0, their prices replaced by dashes.

That ending is the design's weak joint. Once both caps are reached cash has no use in the observed game, the crown stays out of reach, and long-time players' reviews say exactly that: nothing changes after the caps.

7Teaching, interface and feel

The interface is three corners and a road: level number top-left, wallet top-right, two cards at the bottom between runs. Everything else is said by colour and by what happens to the number.

What the player learns, in order

Drag moves the number (hand prompt on Level 1, nothing to fail) → touching numbers grows it (rows of 1s and 2s) → red is bigger than you (side lanes and blockers just above your size) → gates cost value (Level 2's −10/−50 then −100/−20) → pads cross gaps (Level 3) → edges and saws. No text explains any of it; the store page and the colour do.

HUD and states

Persistent: gear and “Level N”, wallet with banknote icon. Pre-run only: START NUMBER and INCOME cards with white or pink prices, tutorial hand. On the road: the number itself is the only score. Settlement: “Level Complete”, the multiplier under the stop wall, a +ticker under the wallet. Failure: “Failed...”.

8Levels are handmade rhythms of the same few parts

Every level number has one fixed layout — Level 1 and Level 2 are identical across two different players and builds. Variety comes from recombining eight parts and from raising the numbers.

PartWhat it asks of the playerSeen with values
Number rowsSweep across to collect; order matters1–10 columns, 5s, 9s, 50s, 77s
Power laddersEat bottom-up so each step is blue in time1 · 2 · 4 · 8 … 64 · 128
Red blockersPass beside, or grow first and eat later150 · 400 · 500 · 600 · 999 · 1200
Gate pairs / banksPick a price; read what waits behind−10 … −111 · −222 · −300 · −555 · −600
Purple dividersCommit to a lane earlyBetween gate lanes and raised lanes
Jump padsLine up before a gap or raised laneSingle pads, one per raised lane
Narrow track / gapsHold a line; avoid drift after gatesBridges, rails, islands
SawsTime or route around slotsStatic and sweeping, in slots

Saws sit in slots across lanes, some sweeping sideways; the store copy tells players to avoid them, but no recorded run touches one, so what contact does is not shown.

Across Levels 1–51 the blockers climb from a few hundred to the high hundreds and beyond, gate prices grow with them, and the stopping walls rise from 600 on Level 1 to 1,800 by Level 13 and 4,500 by Level 30. The starting number grows by a point per purchase while layouts escalate faster, so START NUMBER keeps mattering at the start of each road. A highly upvoted Google Play reviewer reports passing level 500 with all upgrades maxed; an App Store reviewer says the layouts cycle through about twenty levels. Neither claim is visible in the recordings.

9Product, audience and reception

KAYAC's thirteenth hypercasual title rode the 2022 wave of “math runners” to the top of the US charts and still sells the same promise: make big numbers.

The offer

Free on Android and iOS, ad-supported. The store copy is the whole tutorial — “Make big numbers to reach the goal!”, swipe to move, absorb smaller numbers, avoid bigger ones, “avoid electric saws, cross bridges, and jump ditches”, and break the walls at the goal. The App Store subtitle is “Let's go for 1000!”. Google Play lists in-app purchases; the App Store page lists none; one helpful review describes paying to remove ads.

Audience

Declared: anyone who wants a quick “make it bigger” toy. Demanded: one thumb, a fast comparison of two numbers, a little lookahead at gates, tolerance for instant failure, sessions of a minute or a hundred levels. Fit: strong for short play; the long tail strains once upgrades cap and the crown stays unreachable, which is where the critical reviews concentrate.

Development & production

KAYAC dates the launch to October 2022 and announced on 2 December 2022 that the game was #1 among top free games on Google Play in the US, noting refined “accuracy of hits”. The App Store history begins at 0.3.4 (20 Oct 2022); 0.3.8 (11 Nov 2022) added a sound button; 1.0.1 (25 Nov 2022) added levels; 2.0.x (Jan–Mar 2023) brought unspecified new features; later releases are bug fixes through 2.3.6. The two recordings show different builds — one has a SHOP button under the level label, a modified client moves the gear icon — but the same rules.

— Critics
No Metacritic or OpenCritic page and no published outlet reviews found; not on Steam.

Reading it: large samples and high averages say the core toy satisfies casual players. Among the most-upvoted reviews, three complaints recur: ads roughly every other level (skippable after a few seconds), no way to replay a level for a better result, and an end goal (the x777 crown) that feels impossible once upgrades cap. These are player opinions, not measured behaviour, and ratings are not sales evidence.

10What to keep

  • One relation, painted on everything. Colour is never a type; it is the result of comparing two numbers this frame. That makes every pickup, blocker and gate the same lesson.
  • Let costs be seen while they are paid. The counting gate turns an abstract subtraction into a moment the player watches — and the moment a blue number goes red ahead of them.
  • Put the shop where failure lands. Retry opens on the upgrade cards; the blocker that just killed you is visible above them.
  • End the run with a ruler, not a menu. The wall staircase converts a number into spectacle and money in three seconds.
  • Fix the horizon. The source's caps and unreachable crown leave late play without a goal; a rebuild should keep the crown as a real, reachable target.

Build prompt

Build Number Master — a complete mobile-web number runner — as ONE portable HTML file (inline all code, fonts, images and audio; no network, no server). Fantasy: you are a chunky glossy blue number running forward on a white track in an open sky. Drag sideways to steer. Swallow every road number that is not bigger than you (shown blue — it adds to you); never touch one that is bigger (shown red — you shatter). Colours update live as your value changes (R02, R05). Choose which subtraction gate to pay — gates drain you gradually and can drop you under a number that then turns red (R06, fig-drain-1…3, fig-trap-*). Cross gaps with green chevron pads, avoid saws and edges. After the checkered line, ram a staircase of numbered walls; the first wall bigger than you stops you; your final number × INCOME is paid as cash (R12, R13, fig-payout-*). Between levels buy START NUMBER (+1, cap 100) or INCOME (+0.1, cap x6.0) (R15–R17). Deliver the whole game described in "Complete game" below: an endless numbered level sequence with authored layouts and escalation (DS-01), both upgrades with their caps, instant failure and same-level retry, persistence, and a reachable x777 crown as the long-term goal (DS-04, H1). Portrait, one thumb, playable from the first touch and readable without sound; follow the adaptation bridge (#adaptation-bridge), the mobile loop and input map, and design the first 20 minutes with the first-session plan. Keep every Verified rule; design the open items (DS-01…DS-10) so they fit this grammar. Make it look and feel better than the source — crisper numerals, punchier smash and payout, clean audio to the event sheet — without changing what blue and red mean. Plan, build, play-test on a 390×844 touch viewport and fix within this task; a demo, a single level or a promise to finish later is not completion. Report notable design decisions and the acceptance cases you actually ran (#acceptance).

Principles (interpretations from the observed levels)

  • Create situations by moving the line. Layouts put numbers just above the player's likely value so that the order of eating and the choice of gate decide safety. A level is a sequence of “eat this first, then that is blue” moments.
  • Teach by paving, then by margin. Early levels are mostly safe food with red off the main line; red moves into the path only once the player has growth to spend.
  • Escalate numbers, not verbs. The same eight parts recur; difficulty comes from bigger blockers, pricier gates, narrower track and tighter lane commitments.
  • Reward is a ruler. The staircase measures the final number and pays it; there is no losing after the finish line.
  • Failure is information, not punishment. Instant same-level retry on the shop screen. (Exception in the source: no replay of a completed level.)

Core statements

  1. C1 The player sees every road number coloured against their current value and steers to swallow blue ones; each swallow raises the value and re-colours what lies ahead, so route order now changes what is safe later.
  2. C2 At a gate the player chooses a lane price; the gate drains the value while it is crossed and can drop it under a number behind the gate, which turns red — the cheaper-looking choice is only right if the result stays above what follows.
  3. C3 The final value decides how high the number climbs the wall staircase and pays ceil(value × INCOME) in cash; cash buys START NUMBER (a bluer opening next level) or INCOME (more cash per value).
  4. C4 Touching red or leaving the track ends the attempt instantly at no cost; the same level restarts on its upgrade screen, so the next attempt can differ by route and by purchase.

Art direction and signals

Style thesis: toy-bright arithmetic — glossy extruded numerals on a clean white runway floating in an endless blue sky. Keep the source's signal grammar (blue = yours/safe, red = lethal, red gates with white minus labels, green chevron pads, yellow → green → cyan walls under a crown); improve modelling, lighting and motion. Camera: portrait 9:16 window, chase camera behind and above; the player's number sits at ≈60% of screen height so the thumb below never covers it or the next 2–3 rows; HUD only in the top 10% (level left, wallet right); cards and cause chips never overlap the number. Events: swallow = quick squash-and-grow; gate = continuous count with chip spray; red contact = instant break (no anticipation — the read happened before), fragments grey out; wall = heavy burst per wall; payout = drain with coin flight.
